long: Then the fees. Eight. Six. Four.
Larry is made up. The fees are not.
Case file number four. The fee at the end.
Suspect number one. Name: the checkout fee. Aliases: service fee, processing fee, convenience fee.
Last seen: one click before Pay. It never touches the price you see. It waits for the price you pay.
Larry has a ticket in his basket.
To see how the fees got there, we go back to 2015,
to a company that tested them on its own customers.
StubHub, the ticket resale site, was owned by eBay back then.
For a couple of years before that summer, it showed every fee upfront. The price on the screen was the price you paid.
Then, for twelve days in August 2015, it split its buyers in two.
Half kept the full price on screen. The other half saw the ticket alone, with the fees waiting at checkout.
Same tickets. Same fees. The only thing that changed was the moment you saw them.
The ones who met the fees late spent almost twenty-one percent more.
They were fourteen point one percent more likely to buy at all.
And the buyers among them picked seats about five percent pricier.
A seat looks cheaper when its fees are still offstage, so you pick a better one.
Twelve days of science. Then the science went live.
On September the first, the whole site switched. Fees at the end, for everyone.
Larry reads his receipt. Eighteen dollars of fees on a forty-eight-dollar ticket.
That's thirty-seven and a half percent of what he paid.
In September 2025, America's Federal Trade Commission and seven states sued Live Nation and Ticketmaster.
They allege the fees run from twenty-four to forty-four percent of the total price.
And that fans paid over sixteen point four billion dollars in mandatory fees.
Larry's thirty-seven and a half percent sits right inside that range.
His thirty-dollar ticket grew by sixty percent between the first screen and the last.
Larry, it turns out, is perfectly average.
In September 2026, a judge refused to throw the case out. It goes on.
Until a court decides, every word of it is an allegation.
Larry needs a hotel for the concert. Downtown. Nowhere near a beach.
Suspect number two. Name: the resort fee. Aliases: amenity fee, destination fee.
Known associates: a pool you will never swim in.
In 2019, the Attorney General for Washington, D.C., sued Marriott.
The lawsuit says at least one hundred and eighty-nine Marriott hotels charged these fees:
from nine to ninety-five dollars, per room, per day.
Near the end of booking, the fee sat under a heading that sounded official: Taxes and Fees.
From customers in D.C. alone, the Attorney General says, that came to millions of dollars.
Resort fees aren't taxes. They just like to sit next to them.
In 2023, Marriott agreed with Texas to show the total price most prominently.
Why does it work? In 1998, three marketing researchers split prices into a base and a surcharge.
The total price was the same. It was just served in pieces.
People remembered paying less in total. And they bought more.
Your brain files the first number. Everything after it is small print.
If you like catching prices in the act, subscribe. The Inspector has more files.
One: StubHub says it tried honesty.
In 2014, it says, it moved to all-in prices, and lost customers to rivals who kept their fees.
It went back in the fall of 2015.
Two: its own economists saw it differently. Their finding on the switch to late fees: market-expanding, rather than pure business-stealing.
In plain English, hidden fees didn't just win buyers from rivals. They made people spend more.
Three: fees pay for real things. Card payments, staff, the venue.
America's new rule bans no fee at all. It only wants the total, upfront.
The fee may be fair. Hiding it isn't.
Larry's ticket goes on a trip. Three borders. Three stamps.
Border one: America. Since May 2025, ticket sellers and short stays, from hotels to vacation rentals, must show the total price upfront.
In April 2026, StubHub agreed to pay ten million dollars back to buyers,
over fees it showed too late.
America has done this before. In 1958, a law put a sticker on the window of every new car:
the price, every option, the delivery charge, and the total.
Cars got the total sixty-seven years before concert tickets did.
Border two: Britain. Since April 2025, the price must include every fee you can't avoid.
A driving-school group hid a three-pound booking fee charged to over eighty thousand learner drivers.
It paid a four point two million pound fine,
and over seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds in refunds.
In June, StubHub's British arm was fined too.
Border three: the European Union. The total price, taxes included, before you pay.
And any extra charge needs your clear yes. A pre-ticked box is not a yes.
One ticket. Three stamps. One message: show the total.
Three checks before you pay. One. Look for the all-in switch.
Some ticket sites can show prices with fees included. Turn it on before you browse, not after you've fallen for a seat.
Two. Go to the last screen before you decide. The real price lives one click before Pay.
Three. Compare totals, not headlines. A forty-dollar ticket with no fees beats a thirty-dollar ticket with eighteen.
The cheapest ticket is the one with the smallest last number.
Case closed. Larry paid forty-eight dollars for a thirty-dollar ticket.
He went to the concert anyway. The band was worth thirty. The checkout was worth nothing. Now he knows where the eighteen went.
The verdict. Guilty: the checkout fee and its cousin, the resort fee. Accomplice: the first number on the screen.
Next case: the screen that asks how much you'd like to tip, before you've had your coffee.
Subscribe, so the next case file finds you.
